Introduction:
Pre-eclampsia is associated with functional changes in the liver that are thought to resolve after pregnancy [ 1 ], but the long-term risk of developing chronic liver disease has not been studied. Pre-eclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy linked with considerable morbidity and mortality [ 2 , 3 ]. Symptoms range from mild hypertension and proteinuria to severe life-threatening multi-organ dysfunction, including haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome and other hepatic complications [ 4 ]. In extreme cases, pre-eclampsia may result in vasoconstriction of the hepatic vascular bed that is severe enough to cause hepatic necrosis, hematomas, and liver failure or rupture [ 5 ]. Although long-term outcomes have not been studied, many of the acute hepatic effects of pre-eclampsia have the potential to persist after pregnancy or not fully resolve with time. However, there is no information on how pre-eclampsia is related to the subsequent development of chronic liver disease.

A number of studies support the possibility that pre-eclampsia may have a long-term impact on the liver [ 6–8 ]. An analysis of 99 hypertensive pregnant women from Columbia found that residual liver stiffness was common for ≤45 days postpartum [ 6 ]. Studies of men and non-pregnant women suggest that hypertension is a risk factor for liver fibrosis [ 7 , 8 ]—a precursor to chronic liver cirrhosis [ 9 ]. Hypertensive patients are two to three times more likely to develop liver fibrosis over time than normotensive individuals [ 7 , 8 ]. Hypertension is a risk factor for fatty liver disease [ 8 ]. As pre-eclampsia is associated with the development of chronic hypertension over time [ 10 ], our objective was to determine whether pre-eclampsia was associated with the onset of chronic liver disease for up to three decades after pregnancy. We hypothesized that pre-eclampsia increased the risk of developing disorders such as hepatic cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, and fatty liver disease.
Methods:
### Study design and population

We carried out a longitudinal cohort study of 1 460 099 women with and without pre-eclampsia who were pregnant in Quebec, Canada, between 1 April 1989 and 31 March 2022. We extracted the cohort from the Maintenance and Use of Data for the Study of Hospital Clientele registry, which comprises discharge abstracts for all hospital admissions in Quebec, including 98% of deliveries [ 11 ]. We identified the date of admission of the first delivery, determined whether the patient had a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia, and retrieved subsequent hospitalizations for liver disease. Follow-up began at the first delivery and ended on 31 March 2022. We excluded women who did not have a unique patient identifier, as follow-up was not possible. We additionally excluded women who developed liver disease before or during the first pregnancy, to minimize the chance that the association between pre-eclampsia and future liver disease was due to prior hepatic dysfunction.

### Pre-eclampsia

The exposure was pre-eclampsia, defined as hypertension (140/90 mmHg) with new onset of proteinuria or end organ dysfunction developing after 20 weeks of gestation [ 3 ]. The primary exposure measure consisted of pre-eclampsia in any pregnancy compared with no pre-eclampsia. As a secondary exposure, we examined the severity of pre-eclampsia (mild, severe, superimposed). Mild pre-eclampsia was defined as proteinuria of <300 mg/day without eclampsia or a coagulation defect [ 12 ]. Severe pre-eclampsia was defined as significant proteinuria of ≥300 mg/day [ 12 ], eclampsia, or the HELLP syndrome. Superimposed pre-eclampsia consisted of new-onset proteinuria among women with pre-existing hypertension. As an added measure of severity, we categorized pre-eclampsia as early with onset before 34 weeks of gestation or late with onset at 34 weeks or later. Early-onset pre-eclampsia is considered more severe than late onset pre-eclampsia [ 13 ]. We identified women with pre-eclampsia by using diagnostic codes 642.4–642.7, O11, and O13–O15 from the International Classification of Diseases, ninth and tenth revisions ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

We further categorized pre-eclampsia according to first occurrence (first vs. second pregnancy or later) and whether pre-eclampsia occurred more than once. Pre-eclampsia is more common in the first pregnancy, occurring twice as frequently in primigravidas than in women who have previously given birth [ 14 ]. In most patients, pre-eclampsia occurs in the first pregnancy only and does not recur. However, pre-eclampsia may recur in ∼15% of patients in their second pregnancy or in 32% of women in three consecutive pregnancies [ 15 ].

### Outcome

The outcome was hospitalization for non-viral and non-alcoholic liver disease at any time between the first delivery and the end of the study. We included the following liver complications: hepatic cirrhosis, biliary cirrhosis, chronic inflammatory hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, portal hypertension, hepatorenal syndrome, congestive hepatopathy, liver abscess or portal pyaemia, hepatic failure, and liver transplantation. We identified liver outcomes by using diagnostic and procedural codes during admission ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

### Covariates

We included covariates that potentially confounded the relationship between pre-eclampsia and liver outcomes. We accounted for age at first pregnancy (<25, 25–34, ≥35 years), multiple birth, pregnancy comorbidity (gestational or pre-existing diabetes, pre-existing hypertension without superimposed proteinuria, pre-existing dyslipidaemia, obesity, and tobacco, alcohol, or other substance use disorders), socio-economic disadvantage (yes, no, unknown), and time period (1989–99, 2000–10, 2011–22). Socio-economic disadvantage was defined as the lowest quintile of material deprivation, measured as an index of neighbourhood-level income, employment, and education levels [ 16 ]. We placed patients with missing data on socio-economic disadvantage in a separate category for analysis.

### Data analysis

We began by assessing the frequency of pre-eclampsia and liver disease, and computing hospitalization rates for liver disease. In primary analyses, we estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between pre-eclampsia and risk of any liver hospitalization over time. We used Cox proportional-hazards regression models adjusted for age, multiple birth, comorbidity, socio-economic disadvantage, and time period. We used the number of days since the first delivery as the timescale and censored women who died or were never hospitalized for liver disease by the end of the study. We performed the analysis for any pre-eclampsia compared with no pre-eclampsia, as well as according to severity, onset, and recurrence. In a subsequent set of models, we examined the association of pre-eclampsia with specific liver disorders. We used plots of the log (-log survival) curve to confirm that the proportional-hazards assumption was not violated.

In secondary analyses, we examined the association between pre-eclampsia and liver outcomes at different time points during follow-up by using flexible parametric survival models [ 17 ]. In sensitivity analyses, we examined whether associations changed when we included women with a pre-existing history of liver disease, analysed pre-eclampsia as a time-varying exposure, and excluded women with pre-existing hypertension, obesity, or multiple gestations.

We performed the analysis by using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC). The data were anonymized and the study conformed to the Tri-Council Policy Statement on Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans in Canada. The University of Montreal Hospital Centre institutional review board waived ethics review, as informed consent was not needed.
Results:
In this study of 1 460 099 women followed for ≤33 years, 73 018 (5.0%) had pre-eclampsia in one or more pregnancies ( Table 1 ). Among patients with pre-eclampsia, 28.8% had severe, 4.6% had superimposed, and 9.1% had early-onset pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia occurred in the first pregnancy for 79.8% of the patients. A total of 1424 (2.0%) women were hospitalized for a liver disorder during 26 275 081 person-years of follow-up over a median of 18.4 years (interquartile range 9.3–27.8). Among women with pre-eclampsia, a greater proportion were <25 years of age, had a multiple birth, had pregnancy comorbidity, and were socio-economically disadvantaged compared with women without pre-eclampsia.

Women with pre-eclampsia had a higher cumulative incidence of hospitalization for liver disease over time than women without pre-eclampsia ( Fig. 1 ). Hepatic hospitalization rates increased more rapidly within the first 5 years of pregnancy. By the end of follow-up, women with pre-eclampsia had approximately twice the rate of liver hospitalization than women without pre-eclampsia (49.7 vs. 27.9 per 1000 women).

Pre-eclampsia was associated with an elevated risk of liver hospitalization after adjustment for confounders ( Table 2 ). Compared with no pre-eclampsia, women with any pre-eclampsia had 1.85 times the risk of hospitalization for liver disease over time (95% CI 1.75–1.95). Women with superimposed (HR 2.78, 95% CI 2.30–3.36) and early-onset pre-eclampsia (HR 2.36, 95% CI 2.04–2.74) had the greatest risks. Women with a first occurrence of pre-eclampsia in a second or later pregnancy also had an elevated risk of liver hospitalization (HR 1.99, 95% CI 1.79–2.21). Multiparous women with recurrent pre-eclampsia had 3.00 times the risk of liver disease compared with multiparous women without pre-eclampsia (95% CI 2.59–3.46).

Pre-eclampsia was associated with an elevated risk of most liver complications ( Table 3 ). Compared with no pre-eclampsia, women with pre-eclampsia were more likely to be hospitalized for hepatic cirrhosis (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.56–2.27), chronic hepatitis (HR 2.27, 95% CI 2.00–2.57), and fatty liver disease (HR 2.05, 95% CI 1.91–2.20). Women with pre-eclampsia were also at risk of hospitalization for portal hypertension, hepatorenal syndrome, and congestive hepatopathy. There was no clear association with biliary cirrhosis, liver abscess and portal pyaemia, or liver transplantation.

Severe forms of pre-eclampsia were more strongly associated with hepatic cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, and fatty liver disease ( Supplementary Table S2 ). Compared with no pre-eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia was associated with 2.06 times the risk of hepatic cirrhosis (95% CI 1.49–2.85), while superimposed pre-eclampsia was associated with more than three times the risk of chronic hepatitis (HR 3.07, 95% CI 1.95–4.83) and fatty liver disease (HR 3.14, 95% CI 2.47–3.99). Early-onset pre-eclampsia was associated with more than twice the risk of hospitalization for these complications, as well as hepatic failure. Women with recurrent pre-eclampsia had more than three times the risk of any of these outcomes.

Risk of hepatic hospitalization was greatest within 5 years of pregnancy ( Fig. 2 ). Compared with no pre-eclampsia, women with pre-eclampsia had 2.97 times the risk of liver hospitalization 5 years after pregnancy (95% CI 2.37–3.73), 2.62 times the risk 10 years after pregnancy (95% CI 2.22–3.09), and 2.09 times the risk 20 years after pregnancy (95% CI 1.80–2.42). The same pattern was present for hepatic cirrhosis and fatty liver disease.

In sensitivity analyses, pre-eclampsia was associated with a similar risk of hepatic morbidity when we included women with a pre-existing history of liver disease (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.75–1.95) and excluded women with pre-existing hypertension, obesity, or multiple gestations (HR 1.86, 95% CI 1.76–1.98). Associations strengthened slightly with pre-eclampsia as a time-varying exposure (HR 2.40, 95% CI 2.19–2.64).
Discussion:
In this longitudinal cohort study of >1.4 million women, pre-eclampsia was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for liver disease for up to three decades after pregnancy. More severe variants of pre-eclampsia, such as superimposed, early-onset, and recurrent pre-eclampsia, were more strongly associated with the risk of liver hospitalization. Pre-eclampsia was associated with a range of liver complications, including hepatic cirrhosis, chronic inflammatory hepatitis, and fatty liver disease. Risk of hepatic hospitalization was greatest within the first 5 years of pregnancy, although associations persisted throughout the follow-up. The findings suggest that pre-eclampsia—particularly severe, early-onset, and recurrent pre-eclampsia—is associated with the development of liver disease in the long term. These women may benefit from closer clinical follow-up to lower the risk of chronic liver sequelae after pregnancy.

What is known about pre-eclampsia and the liver is limited to the period surrounding pregnancy. In normal pregnancies, blood flow to the liver usually changes minimally, while serum levels of alkaline phosphatase increase due to placental secretion [ 18 ]. Patients with pre-eclampsia, however, may progress to HELLP syndrome, in which hepatic enzymes originating from the liver increase, as does the risk of severe complications such as ischemic liver injury and liver failure [ 18 ]. HELLP syndrome occurs secondary to abnormal placental vascular perfusion and results in endothelial cell dysfunction in several organ systems, including the liver, in which platelet and fibrin deposition in sinusoids can cause hepatocellular necrosis and haemorrhage [ 19 ]. HELLP syndrome is a severe life-threatening maternal morbidity that requires urgent delivery of the foetus [ 20 ]. In the long term, patients with HELLP syndrome have been shown to have adverse outcomes in subsequent pregnancies [ 21 ]. A retrospective review of 128 patients with HELLP syndrome reported that new-onset hypertension and renal failure requiring dialysis were frequent for ≤5 years after pregnancy [ 21 ]. Despite the connection between pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome, studies have not examined long-term hepatic outcomes.

Patients with pre-eclampsia or HELLP syndrome are also at risk of developing acute fatty liver of pregnancy, in which defects in metabolism lead to fatty acid deposits in hepatocytes, causing cellular damage, coagulopathy, and electrolyte imbalance [ 22 ]. The pathways linking pre-eclampsia with acute fatty liver of pregnancy remain to be established, but appear to be distinct from known metabolic defects such as long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, which accounts for only 20% of cases of acute fatty liver of pregnancy [ 22 ]. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is rare but considered an obstetric emergency owing to the risk of multi-organ failure [ 19 ]. A retrospective study of 55 mothers with acute fatty liver of pregnancy found that patients were more likely to experience placental abruption, postpartum haemorrhage, hepatic failure, encephalopathy, and hepatorenal syndrome compared with 220 matched controls with normal liver function [ 23 ]. It is not clear whether these complications are more frequent in patients with pre-eclampsia who develop acute fatty liver of pregnancy, but the general prognosis is that the physiological changes of HELLP syndrome and acute fatty liver return to normal within 2 weeks of delivery [ 22 ]. However, no study appears to have verified this claim. Although damage to the liver may be self-limited, it is possible that mild hepatic injury does not fully resolve after pregnancy and that patients remain at risk of developing chronic liver disease over time.

This possibility would align with data suggesting that endothelial dysfunction due to pre-eclampsia tends to persist following pregnancy [ 24 ]. During gestation, patients with pre-eclampsia have measurable changes in inflammatory cytokines and anti-angiogenic biomarkers that affect endothelial function, arterial blood flow, and blood pressure regulation [ 10 ]. Imbalance in biomarkers such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1) and vascular endothelial growth factor is a fundamental feature of pre-eclampsia [ 10 ]. Biomarkers such as sFlt1 can remain elevated for several years after pregnancy, suggesting that endothelial dysfunction persists in the long term [ 24 ]. Persisting endothelial dysfunction is thought to explain why patients are at risk of developing chronic hypertension over time [ 10 ], including subsequent cardiovascular disease [ 16 ]. Similarly, endothelial dysfunction and chronic hypertension may be mediating factors in the pathway between pre-eclampsia and liver damage, especially sinusoidal injury and fibrosis [ 25 ]. Injured sinusoidal endothelial cells can acquire a vasoconstrictive, inflammatory, and fibrotic phenotype that shifts the liver response towards fibrosis [ 25 ]. In the long term, endothelial dysfunction and chronic hypertension have the potential to lead to chronic liver disease.

Some of the greatest risks were present with hepatic cirrhosis, reinforcing the possibility of a fibrotic effect of pre-eclampsia on the liver. Fibrosis is one of the primary characteristics of cirrhosis [ 9 ]. Severe forms of pre-eclampsia were particularly associated with hepatic cirrhosis, as patients with recurrent pre-eclampsia had more than four times the risk of this complication. Data suggest that endothelial dysfunction may be particularly pronounced in women with multiple episodes of pre-eclampsia [ 26 ], as women with recurrent pre-eclampsia tend to present with greater imbalance in anti-angiogenic biomarkers than women with no recurrence of pre-eclampsia [ 10 ]. Other variants such as severe and early-onset pre-eclampsia were also strongly associated with liver complications after pregnancy.

It has been established that pre-eclampsia is a marker of morbidity later in life [ 10 ], yet clinical practice guidelines on the liver and reproductive health are currently limited to the period surrounding pregnancy [ 19 , 22 ]. Guidelines published by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases address HELLP syndrome and other pregnancy-related complications, but only make recommendations for clinical management during pregnancy [ 19 ]. The guidelines state that liver dysfunction usually resolves shortly after delivery and make no recommendations for long-term follow-up [ 22 ]. Yet, these recommendations appear to be based on the absence of longitudinal investigations, as no study has to date examined the long-term effects of pre-eclampsia on liver function. In this study, we demonstrate that (i) the general belief that liver dysfunction due to pre-eclampsia resolves following pregnancy may be incorrect; and (ii) more research is needed to confirm the possibility that pre-eclampsia may be harmful to the liver by using longitudinal designs. In obstetric medicine, pregnancy is considered a stress test and pre-eclampsia is included in guidelines for long-term cardiovascular risk reduction [ 27 ]. More data are needed to determine whether similar recommendations may apply to the prevention of chronic hepatic disease.

This study has limitations. We used administrative hospital data, which may have been subject to misclassification of exposures or outcomes due to coding errors. Misclassification tends to attenuate differences between groups and result in conservative associations. We could not identify patients who may have received ambulatory care for mild liver disorders or account for patients who left the province during follow-up. Pre-existing liver morbidities may be underreported, as we could not include conditions diagnosed in outpatient settings that were not identified at the time of delivery. We lacked certain patient characteristics, such as ethnicity and medication use. Women with pre-eclampsia may be more likely to use low-dose aspirin or other pharmacological products that affect liver function [ 28 ], thus we cannot rule out residual confounding. We could not analyse potential confounders as time-varying covariates. Although the data are representative of a large multicultural Canadian population with publicly funded healthcare, it is unclear whether the findings can generalize to other communities.

In this longitudinal cohort study of >1.4 million women, pre-eclampsia was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for a range of liver complications, including cirrhosis, hepatitis, and fatty liver disease for up to three decades after pregnancy. Severe forms of pre-eclampsia were more strongly associated with the risk of chronic liver disease. Our findings suggest that women with pre-eclampsia may benefit from closer clinical follow-up to lower the risk of long-term hepatic complications following pregnancy.
